vignette:
He is a 77-year-old North American man who has spent most of his life working with his hands and keeping to routines that make sense to him. He is married, and much of his identity is organized around being dependable: getting up early, doing the route, bringing things where they need to go, and coming home on time. Before the assault, he describes himself as cautious but not fearful, the kind of man who notices the weather, checks his mirrors, and keeps his wallet in the same pocket every day.

The assault happens while he is working his delivery route, in a moment that still feels unreal to him when he tells it. He is making a drop in a neighborhood he knows well, stepping away from the truck with a package in his arms, when he is confronted and attacked. He remembers the shock more than the details at first: the suddenness of it, the loss of control, the force of another person’s aggression entering a day that had felt ordinary. In the weeks afterward, he keeps replaying the moment in fragments. He focuses on small details he cannot stop noticing now—the sound of his shoes on the pavement, the position of his hands, the look on the attacker’s face just before the blow. He feels embarrassed by how long it takes him to pull himself together afterward, and that embarrassment sits beside the fear.

In the first days after the assault, he tries to return to work quickly, partly because he wants to prove to himself that he still can. Instead, the truck begins to feel exposed. He notices every car that slows down behind him, every person standing too still near a doorway, every unfamiliar hand reaching toward him at a delivery stop. He starts taking longer routes, parking farther away, and checking his surroundings repeatedly before getting out. Even when nothing happens, his body acts as if danger is already there. He says his shoulders stay tight all day, his heart jumps too fast at sudden noises, and he is always scanning, as though his mind never fully leaves the assault behind.

At home, he becomes quieter. His wife notices he startles when she comes into a room unexpectedly. He does not like talking about what happened, and when family members ask questions, he gives short answers or changes the subject. He feels irritated with himself for not being “over it” by now, and then guilty for snapping at the people around him. Sleep becomes broken. He falls asleep exhausted, then wakes in the night with the attack in his mind, or with a sense that someone is in the room. Some nights he gets up and sits in the kitchen in the dark, waiting for the feeling to pass. In the morning he feels drained before the day begins.

He also notices that he is not as present with the things he used to enjoy. He still goes to work because he has to, but he does so with less ease and less satisfaction. The job that once gave him structure now feels like something he survives rather than something he does. He avoids certain streets and delivery locations if he can manage it, and he is reluctant to go out in the evening. He no longer lingers with neighbors or chats the way he used to. There is a narrowed quality to his life, as if he is moving carefully through a world that has become unpredictable.

As the months pass, he is troubled by the way the assault seems to live in his body as much as in his memory. A door slamming can bring it all back. A stranger’s raised voice can make him freeze before he can think. He sometimes feels a rush of anger that surprises him, especially when he thinks about how quickly an ordinary workday turned violent. At other times he feels flat and distant, as if he is watching himself from a step away. He says he has always believed in handling things on his own, but this has left him feeling old in a way he did not expect, with a constant sense that he has to stay guarded just to get through the day.

Even now, he keeps working, keeps getting up, keeps driving the route, but the assault remains close to the surface. It shapes how he moves through the world, how he sleeps, how he trusts, and how he measures his own safety from one moment to the next.
